query: The Good Scales {The laboratory has twelve sets of scales and one that's accurate. The queue for it reaches the door.|The queue for the good scales has rules now, chalked on the bench: one weighing each, no hovering, no charms.|The good scales. You can tell from the door how long the wait is by how many people are sighing.} {A third-year at the front is weighing powdered moonstone grain by grain.|The other scales are off by a hair, a whisker or a small mouse.|{season == "summer": It's hot, and every powder in the room is clumping.|The windows have steamed over and nobody can read their numbers.}} Charm your way to the front {You admire the third-year's technique until they wave you ahead out of sheer flattered confusion.|You quote the chalked rules back at the queue in such a reasonable voice that they let you through to weigh "just one thing".|You've learned the queue's weak points. A compliment, a promise and a borrowed spatula, and you're at the scales in a minute.} {The queue turns as one and points at the back. You go to the back.|Someone reads out rule two, NO HOVERING, and looks at you while they do it. The whole queue laughs.|The queue closes ranks like a wall of elbows. You spend the wait at the back, flushed.} Use the bad scales and correct {You weigh everything twice on two bad scales and average the errors. Your measurements are right; your head hurts.|You work out exactly how wrong the mouse-scale is and correct for it. It's tedious, and the best arithmetic you've done all week.|You've mapped all eleven bad scales' errors on a card in your pocket. It doesn't make the work less dull.}
